nodes.title: Versions
nodes.body:
4/4/94.  Ron E. Brockmeyer; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

Common Name:  Gafftopsail catfish
Scientific Name: Bagre marinus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthys
	Order:  Siluriformes
	Family:  Ariidae

OTHER COMMON NAMES:  Gafftop (327), bigmouth catfish (857).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No directed fishery exists, but catfish are often caught incidentally and landed as part of the industrial bottom trawl fisheries (857).

Recreational:  Reported to be a good food fish (327), but not much used (788).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role:  The primarily benthic feeding ariid catfish, may also play an important role as scavengers (165 226 255 908 751 381 857) and as a food source for large predators like juvenile bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas (661)

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Panama and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (891 906 907).  Absent from most of the West Indies (788).

Within Study Area:  Throughout Florida waters including coastal streams (790 835) and throughout the IRL system (848 997 1242).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
This euryhaline, epibenthic, mouth brooder occurs in coastal waters and estuaries, sometimes found in schools (254 255 788 790 848 908).

Movements/Migrations:  Reported to leave the estuaries in the fall to avoid lower water temperatures and return inshore in the spring (252 255 857).  Adults remain in inshore waters year-round in southern Florida (264 603 702).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Nearshore coastal and estuarine waters including waterways, bays, harbors, inlets, channels, canals, grass flats, and fresh water tributaries (788 848 997).

Substrate:  Reported from muddy areas near river mouths (788), and from mud and sand flats (908).  Commonly caught along bridges, piers, and catwalks (788).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs and larvae are carried in the mouth of adult males and the temperature range is that of the adults.

Juvenile/adults:  Juveniles have been collected at temperatures ranging from 10 to 34.9 C (372 550).  Prefer water temperatures 25 C and higher (372 550).  Usually absent at temperatures below 16.5 C (31).  Perret et al (550) caught only one specimen below 20 C.  Thousands of adults died in a cold kill around Sanibel Island at water temperatures ca. 11 C, while adults and juveniles were killed in the IRL where temperatures reached 6-9 C (236).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: Eggs and larvae are carried in the mouth of the males and the salinity range is therefore that of the adult fish.

Juvenile/adults:  Thought to be most abundant at salinities from 5 to 30 ppt (255).  Also recorded from freshwater in Texas (254), in the Caloosahatchee River in southwest Florida (265), and in the Everglades (515 790).  Gilmore (848) found them to be common from freshwater to ocean inlets on the east coast of Florida.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction, oviparous, iteroparous, with the eggs brooded by the males (381 788 909).

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Spawning occurs from May through August in Florida (381 905), probably over mudflats (908).  The eggs and larvae are held in the mouths of adult males (788).

Fecundity:  Reported to range from 20 to 68 eggs/female (381 909)..

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs and yolk sac larvae held in the mouth of adult males for 42 to 70 days (366 908).

Juveniles/Adults:  In Alabama estuaries, Swingle (694) reported growth from 75 mm TL in July to 127 mm TL in September.  Maximum length ranges from 57 cm to 60 cm (312 788), and maximum weight is 2.5 kg (788).  Females are mature at a length of about 265 mm (908).


FOOD HABITS Algae, sea grasses, coelenterates, gastropods, polychaetes, shrimp, crabs and fish are all part of the diet (381 857).  Several authors (165 226 255 908) found that blue crabs are a principal food item.  Juveniles feed on planktonic crustaceans while still in the males mouths (381).  Males apparently do not feed when carrying eggs and larvae in their mouths (788 857).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The primarily benthic feeding ariid catfish, may also play an important role as scavengers (165 226 255 908 751 381 857) and as a food source for large predators like juvenile bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas (661)

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Gafftopsail catfish (Bagre marinus)

FLELMR CODE:  1302

sections.heading: Versions
sections.content:
4/4/94.  Ron E. Brockmeyer; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

Common Name:  Gafftopsail catfish
Scientific Name: Bagre marinus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthys
	Order:  Siluriformes
	Family:  Ariidae

OTHER COMMON NAMES:  Gafftop (327), bigmouth catfish (857).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  No directed fishery exists, but catfish are often caught incidentally and landed as part of the industrial bottom trawl fisheries (857).

Recreational:  Reported to be a good food fish (327), but not much used (788).

sections.heading: Indicator
sections.content: Ecological Role:  The primarily benthic feeding ariid catfish, may also play an important role as scavengers (165 226 255 908 751 381 857) and as a food source for large predators like juvenile bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas (661)

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Coastal waters from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Panama and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (891 906 907).  Absent from most of the West Indies (788).

Within Study Area:  Throughout Florida waters including coastal streams (790 835) and throughout the IRL system (848 997 1242).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
This euryhaline, epibenthic, mouth brooder occurs in coastal waters and estuaries, sometimes found in schools (254 255 788 790 848 908).

Movements/Migrations:  Reported to leave the estuaries in the fall to avoid lower water temperatures and return inshore in the spring (252 255 857).  Adults remain in inshore waters year-round in southern Florida (264 603 702).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Nearshore coastal and estuarine waters including waterways, bays, harbors, inlets, channels, canals, grass flats, and fresh water tributaries (788 848 997).

Substrate:  Reported from muddy areas near river mouths (788), and from mud and sand flats (908).  Commonly caught along bridges, piers, and catwalks (788).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs and larvae are carried in the mouth of adult males and the temperature range is that of the adults.

Juvenile/adults:  Juveniles have been collected at temperatures ranging from 10 to 34.9 C (372 550).  Prefer water temperatures 25 C and higher (372 550).  Usually absent at temperatures below 16.5 C (31).  Perret et al (550) caught only one specimen below 20 C.  Thousands of adults died in a cold kill around Sanibel Island at water temperatures ca. 11 C, while adults and juveniles were killed in the IRL where temperatures reached 6-9 C (236).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae: Eggs and larvae are carried in the mouth of the males and the salinity range is therefore that of the adult fish.

Juvenile/adults:  Thought to be most abundant at salinities from 5 to 30 ppt (255).  Also recorded from freshwater in Texas (254), in the Caloosahatchee River in southwest Florida (265), and in the Everglades (515 790).  Gilmore (848) found them to be common from freshwater to ocean inlets on the east coast of Florida.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction, oviparous, iteroparous, with the eggs brooded by the males (381 788 909).

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
Spawning occurs from May through August in Florida (381 905), probably over mudflats (908).  The eggs and larvae are held in the mouths of adult males (788).

Fecundity:  Reported to range from 20 to 68 eggs/female (381 909)..

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs and yolk sac larvae held in the mouth of adult males for 42 to 70 days (366 908).

Juveniles/Adults:  In Alabama estuaries, Swingle (694) reported growth from 75 mm TL in July to 127 mm TL in September.  Maximum length ranges from 57 cm to 60 cm (312 788), and maximum weight is 2.5 kg (788).  Females are mature at a length of about 265 mm (908).


FOOD HABITS Algae, sea grasses, coelenterates, gastropods, polychaetes, shrimp, crabs and fish are all part of the diet (381 857).  Several authors (165 226 255 908) found that blue crabs are a principal food item.  Juveniles feed on planktonic crustaceans while still in the males mouths (381).  Males apparently do not feed when carrying eggs and larvae in their mouths (788 857).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: The primarily benthic feeding ariid catfish, may also play an important role as scavengers (165 226 255 908 751 381 857) and as a food source for large predators like juvenile bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas (661)
